query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the aging heat treatment (e.g., near 750°C for 24 hours with adjusted cooling parameters to minimize coarsening) will induce a uniform dispersion of fine and coherent Ni3Ti precipitates in the Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing its elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance by approximately 30–50% compared to the homogenized, untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast and homogenized Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy with composition approximately Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Nb 13.3 at%, Mo 13.3 at%, and Cr 13.3 at%.
generation.intervention: A post-solidification aging heat treatment designed to precipitate nickel-titanium intermetallic (Ni3Ti) phases.
generation.conditions: The homogenized cast alloy is aged at approximately 750°C for 24 hours in an inert atmosphere, followed by controlled cooling. Aging parameters are to be optimized to achieve a fine, stable precipitate distribution with minimal coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: A fine, uniformly distributed, and coherent dispersion of Ni3Ti precipitates embedded within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Ni3Ti precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and inhibit grain-boundary sliding, thereby increasing the yield strength and creep resistance of the material at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy will exhibit a measurable improvement in high-temperature mechanical properties, such as a 30–50% increase in yield strength and enhanced creep resistance, relative to the control alloy that has not undergone the aging treatment.
generation.baseline: The control alloy is a fully homogenized cast alloy without any post-solidification aging, showing lower yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloys within the defined compositional range (each primary element between 5–35 at%) and is intended for use in elevated temperature environments (approximately 600–800°C) where mechanical performance is critical.
generation.uncertainty: Precise optimization of the aging parameters is needed to ensure optimal fine precipitate formation without coarsening over time. Long-term stability of the precipitates under sustained high-temperature conditions remains uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with the specified composition. Subject one set to the optimized aging treatment (750°C for 24 hours with controlled cooling) and leave the other set in the homogenized state without aging. Conduct microstructural characterization and mechanical testing on both sets.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to confirm the presence, size, and uniformity of Ni3Ti precipitates.
Hardness testing to assess any improvement in surface or bulk hardness.
High-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength and creep tests at ~700°C) to quantify the improvements in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and creep resistance (i.e., less than ~30% improvement) compared to the homogenized control, or if the intended Ni3Ti precipitate formation is not confirmed by microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

proposals.material_system: Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Nb 13.3 at%, Mo 13.3 at%, Cr 13.3 at%)
proposals.intervention: Post-solidification aging heat treatment to induce coherent Ni3Ti (L1₂) precipitate formation
proposals.conditions: Homogenized cast alloy is aged at 750°C for 24 hours under an inert atmosphere, followed by controlled cooling
proposals.structural_mediator: Fine, uniformly distributed Ni3Ti precipitates embedded within the matrix
proposals.mechanism: Precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., a 30–50% increase in yield strength and creep resistance) relative to the same alloy in a fully homogenized state
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By making titanium and nickel the primary constituents and inducing a strengthening precipitate phase (instead of treating them merely as additions), this approach directly targets the microstructural mechanism to boost high-temperature performance in a HEA design that has not been previously explored.

proposals.material_system: Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Nb 13.3 at%, Mo 13.3 at%, Cr 13.3 at%)
proposals.intervention: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) followed by low-temperature annealing to engineer an ultrafine-grained structure
proposals.conditions: The cast alloy is subjected to high-pressure torsion at room temperature, then annealed at 500°C for 1 hour to stabilize submicron and high-angle grain boundaries
proposals.structural_mediator: Refined, nanocrystalline grains with stabilized high-angle grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Grain refinement increases grain-boundary strengthening and restricts dislocation movement, which is crucial for maintaining mechanical integrity at high temperatures
proposals.predicted_outcome: Enhanced elevated-temperature strength and creep resistance due to the refined microstructure, with average grain sizes reduced below 1 μm compared to a baseline with several microns grain size
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach leverages microstructural control via deformation processing to optimize performance, specifically in a HEA where Ti and Ni are major constituents, addressing the untested design space with a mechanism distinct from compositional modifications

proposals.material_system: Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy modified with a minor interstitial addition (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Nb 13 at%, Mo 13 at%, Cr 13 at%, plus 1–2 at% C)
proposals.intervention: Intentional addition of carbon to promote in-situ formation of TiC carbide particles during solidification
proposals.conditions: The alloy is cast under controlled cooling rates that favor homogeneous TiC nucleation and growth, with carbon levels maintained at 1–2 at% (keeping all elements within the 5–35 at% window)
proposals.structural_mediator: Nano-scale TiC precipitates distributed primarily at grain boundaries and within the matrix
proposals.mechanism: Dispersion strengthening by fine TiC carbides, which hinder grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby enhancing mechanical performance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Significant improvement in creep resistance and yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., measurable increases compared to a carbon-free baseline), with clear TiC phase identification using TEM and XRD
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention specifically capitalizes on in-situ particle formation in a titanium–nickel primary HEA, directly addressing the gap in exploring such compositions and novel strengthening routes in this material system

proposals.material_system: Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti 30 at%, Ni 30 at%, Nb 13.3 at%, Mo 13.3 at%, Cr 13.3 at%)
proposals.intervention: Surface nitriding treatment to form a hardened titanium nitride (TiN) layer
proposals.conditions: The alloy’s surface is treated in a nitrogen-rich atmosphere at 500°C for 6 hours, ensuring nitrogen diffusion and TiN formation without affecting the bulk composition
proposals.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent TiN surface layer with minimal penetration depth (~several microns)
proposals.mechanism: The hard and thermally stable TiN phase formed on the surface acts as a protective barrier against oxidation and wear, while also contributing to improved high-temperature mechanical integrity
proposals.predicted_outcome: Enhanced surface hardness, oxidation resistance, and fatigue performance at elevated temperatures compared to the untreated alloy, as confirmed by hardness testing and high-temperature oxidation assays
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This surface engineering strategy offers a distinct mechanism—modifying only the near-surface microstructure—to improve overall high-temperature performance in a HEA with titanium and nickel as primary constituents, thus navigating an unexplored aspect of the compositional space

critiques.addresses_problem: Partially; it targets oxidation and surface wear aspects that can deteriorate mechanical performance at elevated temperatures but may not address bulk creep or fatigue mechanisms.
critiques.constraints: Respects the composition constraint as it only modifies the surface without altering the bulk elemental ratios.
critiques.physical_soundness: Physically sound in terms of forming a protective, thermally stable TiN layer on a titanium‐rich surface, but the effect is limited to the near-surface region.
critiques.feasibility: Feasible using established surface nitriding procedures with controlled nitrogen atmospheres and temperatures.
critiques.evidence: Related studies on oxidation resistance improvements via passivating element additions support surface modifications (see records PMC9498035 and PMC7040784), though direct evidence for TiN on this specific HEA is not provided.
critiques.main_risk: The treatment may not enhance the bulk high-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., creep or yield strength) and could fail if the degradation mechanisms are primarily internal rather than surface-initiated.
critiques.fix: Combine the surface nitriding with a complementary bulk treatment, or optimize the nitriding depth to ensure a more significant influence on overall mechanical integrity at elevated temperatures.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes; it directly improves high-temperature strength and creep resistance by refining the grain structure, which is a well-known mechanism for strength improvement.
critiques.constraints: Meets the compositional requirement without altering the nominal elemental percentages and operates within the established processing conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: Mechanistically sound: severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing yields an ultrafine-grained structure that enhances strength via grain-boundary strengthening.
critiques.feasibility: Feasible with current techniques like high-pressure torsion and controlled annealing, as demonstrated in various HEA studies.
critiques.evidence: Several studies (e.g., records PMC10744552 and PMC10744483) indicate that grain refinement via severe plastic deformation can significantly enhance mechanical properties of HEAs.
critiques.main_risk: The refined ultrafine grains might coarsen at elevated service temperatures, reducing the long-term mechanical benefits.
critiques.fix: Introduce grain boundary stabilization mechanisms (such as minor additions that inhibit grain growth) to maintain the ultrafine structure during prolonged high-temperature exposure.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes; incorporating a minor interstitial addition of carbon to form in-situ TiC particles directly targets improved high-temperature strength via dispersion strengthening in the Ti–Ni primary HEA.
critiques.constraints: Respects the compositional window since the carbon addition is minor (1–2 at%) and does not shift the primary elemental ratios out of the 5–35 at% range.
critiques.physical_soundness: Physically sound: nanoscale TiC precipitates can effectively hinder dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, enhancing creep resistance and yield strength at elevated temperatures.
critiques.feasibility: Feasible with controlled casting and cooling methods that promote homogeneous TiC nucleation, which are well established in alloy processing.
critiques.evidence: Relevant studies on carbide precipitation and dispersion strengthening in similar titanium-rich alloys (e.g., insights from PMC11549039 and PMC9571103) support the rationale, although direct evidence in this exact HEA system is limited.
critiques.main_risk: There is a risk of excessive or inhomogeneous TiC formation, which could lead to embrittlement or unwanted segregation if not precisely controlled.
critiques.fix: Fine-tune the carbon content and cooling rate to ensure uniform nanoscale precipitation and avoid overgrowth or agglomeration of TiC particles.

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes; inducing the formation of coherent Ni3Ti precipitates is a recognized method to boost yield strength and creep resistance, directly targeting the elevated-temperature performance in Ti–Ni primary alloys.
critiques.constraints: The intervention adheres to the compositional constraint by relying on the existing primary constituents (Ti and Ni) without introducing extraneous elements, and the aging conditions are within feasible operating boundaries.
critiques.physical_soundness: Physically sound: coherent precipitates such as Ni3Ti effectively obstruct dislocation motion, enhancing strength; however, the stability of the precipitates at prolonged high temperatures must be ensured.
critiques.feasibility: Feasible using standard aging heat treatments and homogenization processes that are common in alloy development, as evidenced by similar practices in related HEA systems.
critiques.evidence: Studies (e.g., records PMC8074761 and PMC10708198) show that precipitation of secondary phases like sigma or ordered phases improves high-temperature strength; while Ni3Ti specifically is less documented in HEAs, the underlying mechanism is analogous.
critiques.main_risk: The Ni3Ti precipitates might coarsen over time or dissolve under service conditions, potentially reducing the intended strengthening effect.
critiques.fix: Optimize aging parameters (temperature and time) to achieve a stable, fine dispersion of Ni3Ti precipitates that resist coarsening during prolonged high-temperature exposure.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly targets the bulk mechanical performance at elevated temperatures by employing a post-solidification aging treatment to induce the formation of coherent Ni3Ti precipitates. This approach leverages the primary Ti–Ni interaction in the alloy to provide in situ precipitation strengthening. Although there is a risk of precipitate coarsening, the critique suggests this risk is manageable through optimization of the aging parameters, which makes the approach both physically sound and feasible. Compared to the other directions, this method more directly addresses the creep resistance and yield strength improvement necessary for high-temperature applications in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
